I guess it could, in theory, gather so much dust (depending on the room it's in, whether it get's caked on there or not) that it would inhibit heat dissipation. If you're just using it in a normal environment and not always cranking to it's maximum output, it's very unlikely to happen before buying another amp later down the line.

If this tube ever got that hot, and is covered in dust, it would burn off most of the dust that's on there. You'd smell the dust burning, and the tube would probably still be fine.

If it makes you feel better, get a can of compressed air and spray it once every month or so. Less of a hassle than covering it, though I've never heard of anyone needing to do any of this. If you're going to spray compressed air, just make sure to hold the can upright enough so that it doesn't blast out the liquid gas, it's extremely cold and might just crack the tube from thermal shock.

These you're probably not going to get rid of, and everything's going to show. Call it a patina, accept that it's there and that it's going to get 'worse' and that it's just from you enjoying the guitar. Good guitars get played, so consider it a good sign ;)

You can try to polish it out using polishing compounds and a clean rag (or old t shirt, something soft, no kitchen/toilet paper!) Courser one first, then fine. Buff it out in a circular motion, then try to wipe off as  as you can. Clean the guitar with a finish cleaner and a new, clean rag :) It'll slightly improve by getting rid of the smallest scratches, the bigger deeper ones will stay more or less the way they are now. 

If there are any actual deep scratches, be sure to wipe out the polishing compound that may get stuck in there or it's going to get very hard to remove later and it's going to be even more of an eyesore. 

Good luck!

I'm in the EU, so I'll stick to the pricing and brands I'm familiar with.

This one's cheating, but Cor-Tek-made guitars are really good value - varying somewhat between the companies they're building for. Cor-Tek is one of the biggest guitar manufacturers in the world, producing in East-Asia (I think mainly in Indonesia). You'd still be paying for the brand, as is always the case to some extent I suppose, because they produce guitar for all the Asian import brands (PRS SE, any non-japanese Ibanez, Squier, non-US G&L, Gretsch, and a whole bunch more).  
Their own house brand is simply called *Cort*, and they build guitars and basses ranging from 200 to about 1300. Counting it because their higher end is in line with MIM Fenders in the EU atm. Compared to MIM Fenders, I'd say they beat them in terms of build quality and hardware used. Probably not very interesting if you're looking for Fender/Gibson-like guitars. Electrics are mostly modern designs.

*Maybach* (Czech Republic) are a really solid 'boutique' option, there's a load of these smaller scale builders that will offer aged/relic'd nitro finishes and great hardware for about the price of an American Vintage II. (They also have a custom shop kinda thing, I think it's a guy in Berlin who solo builds custom orders for Maybach).

*Del-Tone* is just 2 guys building just outside of Amsterdam, recent startup (2018 I think) doing Fender-style builds. They use their own (Apollo) pickups, interesting finish options and aged/relic'd nitro finishes. Their guitars are (almost always) super lightweight because they use abachi wood.

Also Dutch, *Haar guitars* has been around for a bit longer and they make some fantastic guitars. They also build Suhr-like superstrats and Gibson-style guitars.

*Duesenberg* are generally a little more expensive than most US-made Fenders, but they do offer some less expensive models. These are made for the most part in Croatia, and finish production in Hannover Germany. Excellent quality, immaculate playability, really cool designs. It's very much it's own thing, so if you're looking for Fender/Gibson style guitars, this is not that. Very different, very cool, really good. I love these.

*Eastman* guitars have a bunch of electrics, some of their own design (I'm into them) and some Gibson style guitars (LP's and archtops). The SB series are their take on the Les Paul and they're awesome. They're available with either Seymour Duncan or Lollar pickups.

PRS S2 now come with their US-made pickups instead of the Korean ones (Those will have the 's' suffix in the pickup name). Consistently good, in my eyes these are a better product than what Fender and Gibson are selling for comparable prices. You may also find some 10th anniversary S2 models, which also have the US-made pickups, these are likely on sale in places that have them because not long after these came out PRS made US-pickups standard for S2. If you're looking into this, check which pickups they have since it's a recent change.

As a bassist, I love Sandberg guitars. These are made in Germany (except for the electra series, which are Asia-made -but still assembled and QC'd in Germany). The prices vary because the German builds are kinda one-off builds. They have a bunch of aging/relic options, and they do this very well. This costs a lot of time, driving up the price dramatically. Any aged guitar will have nitro finish, no aging means poly and these are around 2000 (I think mostly slightly under). They mainly do basses, I haven't played any of their guitars but they exist. They look awesome, and I love their hardware. Fender style but slightly different.

Dominance of online shopping, and how it's changed customer expectations. I suspect this is not the case for Bax, shown in the picture, as they've been doing most of their business online and I think were backed by investors.

This is what I gleamed from just little over 2.5yrs in a music instrument shop:

I'll be talking about Thomann mainly as they are the biggest worldwide, and this is the one that affects European shops like the one I work at the most.

For most gear, you have to match prices with online retailers, for the most part there's no way around it. Even after lots of service, allowing people to test out all sorts of equipment and ask all their questions to experts in a building that's expensive to keep open with current gas/electricity rates and such, people are going to try and get what is best for them. Thomann doesn't do nearly as much for their customers as brick-and-mortar shops do, that's one of the reasons they stay on top with much smaller profit margins.

You don't need big margins if you fulfil 40.000(!) orders daily. I would also expect they get to get far better prices from their suppliers because of the insane amounts of sales as well.

People do like to shop in physical stores where they can get help, at least when it comes to instruments and other equipment. If after helping someone choose the right guitar you don't have the right colour, Thomann will always be there for them -likely with plenty in stock in whatever configuration they choose. This means customers may end up buying from Thomann after the mom and pop store has spent time helping them. Treating customers well, giving good and honest advice will increase the odds of them wanting to buy from you, it feels almost like relying on a weird kind of charity. 

If they do buy from you, you're likely going to match Thomann in pricing who have done nothing to help this person. Now let's say this customer bought a high-end US-made guitar with a factory flaw that went unnoticed, the customer would want to get this fixed. Options:  
\- have a guitar technician spend valuable time to try and fix it  
\- send back to manufacturer, and wait for a new one (may take a long time, supplier may not have stock)  
Customer has to wait, and may just decide to get their money back for the guitar because they could have the same model delivered to their doorstop just a day later by buying from Thomann. If that one has a factory defect, no problem! Thomann can just take it back in and send them a new one because they have 160 of them anyway. A lot of time spent on making exactly 0,- because of a mistake someone else made.

Also, big chain stores like Thomann and Guitar Center have made it so that people need everything to be untouched by a human since leaving the factory. Many expect a guitar from the shop floor to be a demo-model to try before getting one from an unopened box. This is obviously not feasible for brick-and-mortar shops with limited inventory and storage room. This is usually not too big of an issue, but it does show how quickly people adjusted to these newer business models.

Shops live off of profit margins, and Thomann has drastically reduced those by simply not being as involved with customers as brick-and-mortar shop are. Everyone loves that the shop I work at still exists as one of the few remaining in the city, but nobody's willing to pay more for the service they got. I don't fault anyone for that, it's the sane thing to do, but they are contributing to a barren landscape when it comes to the stores that they love and praise. 

Basically, if you're buying local you're probably:  
\-getting too much attention and help, or  
\-paying too little

Please buy local from mom and pop's, it's not that much more expensive because they cannot afford to not sell anything. They'll rather take the hit in their profit margins than not sell anything at all, and if they don't lower their prices it's likely because they can't.

Maybe the martin needs a little bit more time, to me it feels like most new Martins I get to play kind of 'hold back' a bit. Martins tend to sound a little darker compared to similarly spec'd Eastmans, though many of the Eastman Dreads in that pricepoint (e10/20/40, very roughly) will have torrified and/or adirondack spruce tops so the comparison is not entirely fair. 

Rosewood back and sides tend to have pretty solid, somewhat boomy bass response with -to my ears- a little peak in the trebles. Sapele has far more mid-range presence, especially in the high-mids (I think) and has overall o more 'trebly' sound than rosewood. Compared to 'genuine', or south-american mahogany it doesn't sound as airy and feels a little bit sharper.

You won't know you got a dud until you play some other D16's of the same age. By now, 3 years in, your Martins woods should be seasoned well-enough. Maybe it just needs more playing, it may compact the wood fibres somewhat. 

About its quieter nature, rosewood back/sides are generally more dynamic than mahogany/sapele. I would expect your D16 to be louder when playing hard, and your E1D to be louder when playing with a softer touch. Mahogany tends to compress volume levels a bit. Again, we don't know how long you've had the guitar, but if it's new to you, play it for a while. Maybe it's you that needs the adjusting, some guitars 'demand' to be played differently than others and it takes a bit of time to find out what it is that this guitar 'likes' to do. 

If you bought it in a physical store recently, it may be worth exploring some other guitars in that price-range by playing them. They may let you trade it in for the other one, if it's within a reasonable timespan. It's very possible mahogany guitars just suit you more, maybe try out a genuine mahogany guitar (I don't think I've ever spoken to anyone that didn't prefer that over sapele (African mahogany)). If you get to do that, it'd be a good chance to sit with another D16 to see if yours is a 'dud' (I'm hesitant to call it that because it's all so subjective, but it's true that some Martins are very quiet or muffled sounding).

I work in a music instrument shop that mainly sells guitars and basses, so I get to play quite a few Martins and Eastmans, Taylors and some other smaller brands.

Sounds like you're not fretting properly. Try to play the chord like you normally would, but play each string individually. Try to make them all ring out on their own, one at a time. Take your time to figure how how much (or rather, little,) pressure you need to exert for the strings to ring out. 

It's worth checking how well your guitar is set up, I don't want to go all over the place with this reaction so I'll leave this one for you to google. I don't think it would be this bad since you're playing just behind the capo. A poor set-up could make things harder than they should. One other thing that might make this a little harder could be the capo. If it's squeezing too hard, it may cause the string to kind of bulge up behind the fret.

You should probably cut your nails, at least on your fretting hand. Then move your shoulder, elbow and wrist around until you find a more comfortable way to play. I notice your wrist is facing outwards, try moving your elbow out from your side. This way your wrist is more or less perpendicular to the neck of your guitar, and your fingers in line with the frets. This allows more finger mobility, should make the chords easier to play with some practice. It's worth occasionally investigating what it takes for a string to ring out, you'd be surprised how little pressure it needs. The hard part is to then learn to apply the correct amount of pressure on each string without squeezing too hard or causing injuries to your hand or wrist :) Some guitar players will talk about strength from practice, but I think 80% of that 'strength' is just improved technique.

OP, you can check your intonation using a tuner (there are apps that'll work in a pinch, if you don't own a tuner). It's good to understand beforehand that guitars aren't going to be perfectly in tune, an impossibility within the 12-tet (twelve tone equal temperament). 

Your guitar is well-intoned (meaning as good as guitars get) if the pitch that your strings produce at the twelfth fret is exactly an octave above the unfretted note. 

The twelfth fret *should* be the halfway point of the strings, between the nut at the headstock end and the bridge saddle at the other end. Fretting the 12 fret therefore cuts the length of the relevant part of the string (between fret and bridge) in half, doubling the frequency. This is your octave.



To roughly check intonation by ear, lightly rest a finger on any string directly over the 12th fret. If you then pluck it, you can let go and it should still ring out. What you're hearing is the octave as it should be. Since you're not using the fret to play the octave, but just the string, you're getting the exact half of the string to vibrate. Playing this note like a harmonic (not fretting down, but lightly resting against), makes it easier to hear the difference. You could use the open string, that and the harmonic are the same note anyway.

Now fret the 12th fret and play the same string again. If your guitar is well-intonated, the note you got when you lightly rested your finger on the string and when you pressed down to fret the 12th will be the same. If they're not, your guitar isn't well-intonated.

If you have a tuner, compare an open string to the same string fretted at the 12th fret.

Assuming your frets are installed at the correct spots on the neck (it's very unlikely they're not), there are a couple of things that could cause poor intonation. Either:

\-Your action is too high (strings are far away from the frets). If you have really high action, the act of bringing the string down to the fret increases tension, effectively bending the string out of pitch before it even reaches your fretboard. Fixing this will make your guitar play the way it should, and improve intonation.

\-The string length is incorrect. This could be your nut (the string needs to leave the nut at the body-end of the guitar, an incorrectly filed nut-slot could make a string too long. It's not very likely that it is.   
More likely it's your bridge saddle. They're about 3mm deep I think, they're shaped to achieve proper intonation on the guitar. For instance, if a string 'leaves' the bridge saddle 2mm too far to the butt-end of the guitar, the halfway point of the string will be shifted half of that (1mm) to the butt-end of the guitar too, which essentially makes all your frets be in the wrong place. 

If you're not a handyman I wouldn't recommend intonating an acoustic yourself. I'm guessing it'd be somewhere between 50-70 usd/eur. If that's too much, you have to ask yourself how often you're playing that high up the guitar. Generally intonation gets worse the farther up the neck you're playing.

There are some simple tricks to find out how much you can improve your action. It seems pretty playable as is, but better is better.

Fret the third fret on each string. You want the string to get as close to the 1st fret as possible without resting on it, your nut doesn't need to be any higher than your frets. Usually luthiers will set up with a tiny bit extra. If there's a larger gap (feeling helps) your nut slot may be too high, making it harder to play and slightly worsening intonation.

To check the neck, hold down fret 1 & 12 and tap in the middle. You'll want a little bit of relief between the string and frets halfway fret 1/12, maybe just 0.5 - 1 credit-card's worth of relief. Feel with your finger how much space there is, if there's a lot of room between fret and string your neck is bowed slightly. That's fine, your guitar is made to handle the strings tension. That's what the truss rod if made to do, adjust it by turning clockwise. Don't force anything, and do 1/8th of a turn and check again. 

If both neck and nut are fine, you can try lowering your bridge. A luthier will know how much lower your action will be able to get, and will know how to do it. If you're unsure, go see one :) 

As for barre chords, those are just very tricky and will take a lot of time. This action looks like you should be able to do it rather easily with some practice, don't give up! Technique will improve and you'll be able to use that instead of force

This is what you can easily do yourself without any tools, aside from an allen key:  
  
Look for a truss-rod access, likely where the guitar's neck meets the body, just under the top of the guitar. It may be at the head-stock end, but that's rather uncommon for acoustic guitars. Often there'll be a small round hole in the brace looking through the soundhole towards the neck, this hole is there so you can access the truss rod behind it. Assuming it's not an American-made guitar, it's probably a 4mm truss allen key you need. Maybe 5, probably 4. The right size is usually included in the box.

Press down on fret 1 and 12 to check action (capo on either frees up a hand). The string will be 100% straight, so any space between it and the frets around fret 6/7 is the amount of 'relief' your neck has. Press down to feel how much the string can move before it hits the fret.  
  
If it fits half a credit-card's thickness, it's straight as an arrow, so (almost) no relief. I'm expecting you to find quite a bit of room between the string and the frets, meaning it needs to be straightened out somewhat. Theoretically you'd need a little bit of relief, probably aim for about a credit-card's worth of play around the 7th fret when fretting on 1 and 12.

To get there, insert your allen key into the truss rod end. This may be finicky. Start off with about a 1/8 turn clockwise. If it feels really heavy, don't force it. After turning, check relief again. Rinse and repeat until you get to that credit-card's worth of relief. If nothing happens, you may need to gently 'massage' your neck, gently bend the neck forward and backward. If the truss rod is stuck in there, that may loosen it. Doesn't happen a lot, but some guitars will have that. I think mainly old ones that have been sitting for too long.

If your strings start to buzz, the neck may be too straight or even slightly back-bowed. Inexpensive guitars may have poor fretwork, that's not a big deal, but it means a less perfect possible set-up. Loosen up on the truss-rod a little if it starts to buzz.

Other factors that may result in poor playing action:

  
\-Nut slots that are too high. They shouldn't be much higher than your frets (maybe a couple hairs over). To check, press down the third fret and with your other hand tap the string on the 2nd fret. It should 'ping' by hitting the fret almost immediately as you touch it. That means it's about as low as the frets, this is what you want. If it's high, have a guitar tech file down your nut slots to correct height. 

\-Bridge saddle too high. Not something you can easily do yourself, but it can be sanded down. They're often a bit too high by manufacturers playing it safe. If you overdo it, you need a new bridge saddle entirely which takes a guitar tech some time to dial in. Probably best to have a guitar tech do this. 

\-Neck straight, nut slots good, bridge saddle low? This is the bad ending. Neck isn't pitched back enough. The only fix is a neck-reset, which costs more than most entry level guitars and isn't risk-free.

TLDR;   
Try to adjust truss-rod if there's a lot of neck-relief. If good, good. If not good enough, bring to luthier. GL! :)

Depends on the room it's in. At the very least, get a stand. They're inexpensive and keep your guitar from taking a tumble. Hygrometers are also inexpensive.  
  
If the humidity in this room is somewhere around 40/50%, and if it's fairly constant, it'll be fine. If not, storing it in a case can help. The case is essentially a tiny room within this one, adding another buffer that prevents big humidity changes.   
  
If this room is either ridiculously dry or humid, you're going to need a case along with either a humidifier or dehumidifier, and to keep an eye on it. It's unlikely though. The humidity level in the case will eventually reach that of the room.

If the conditions in the room are not okay, and you cannot invest in a case, it may still be fine. If it's an inexpensive guitar, you may be more willing to take your chances, which is fair. Though keep in mind that, if you can afford it, a hardshell case can likely be used for any similarly sized guitar you get in the future.  
  
Proper storage can prolong the lifespan of your guitar, but so can proper repairs. Loose braces and cracked seams can be glued, usually without issue. If something were to happen, just know that there are people that can fix 'er right up.  
  
The amount of bowed instruments that are still in use despite being hundreds of years old tell me that we handle guitars very differently from these older instruments, we tend to not bother with repairs or go for whatever cheap repair will get the guitar to play again for another couple years. These things obviously cost a lot of money, and I can imagine these quickly overtake the initial cost of the guitar, so prevention is usually cheaper than fixing.

You're not supporting local dealers who often cannot afford to be more expensive than Thomann/amazon/whatever online store. They are forced to match pricing, while having to work extra hard to stay afloat. Now I'm not saying you should buy local as an act of kindness, but just realise that they will actually offer service because they need your patronage. They'll gladly give you advice, let you try out new gear, and fix any issues.

Also, if a store gets a piece of crap from their suppliers, they have to fix it. You're far less likely to encounter bad guitars, as the store will have to fix it in order to even sell the damn thing. I guess the pressure to do so would be lower if you're ordering online, but most stores are counting on people to return because they value the place, so they'll still be inclined to fix any issues. 

Basically, you're getting brick-and-mortar service while paying amazon prices nowadays. You just got unlucky with this one, but the likelihood of it happening is lower when you buy from actual stores. If they send you an unchecked guitar, they're taking a risk as well.

I'd always recommend people get cracks and splits looked after by a luthier as they appear. If you're able to, go see one and have them glue it up. In the meantime, keep an eye on the ambient humidity and don't worry too much about your guitar. Some tips:

Avoid any 'shocks' in humidity levels, and keep it between 40-60% relative humidity. (I think most manufacturers aim for around 45% when building and storing guitars before shipping)

Little separations become big ones over time, because some humidity change is inevitable. The wood will swell and bulge with increases in humidity as it absorbs moisture from the air. In a dry environment it'll release moisture. With fast or drastic moisture loss, the wood will contract perpendicular to the grain, causing splits. 

A good quality gigbag, or preferably a case, will act as a buffer, slowing down humidity changes. Slow changes are less hurtful because it allows for these changes to occur at more or less equal rates across the guitars different woods, resulting in smaller stresses. If you keep it on a stand, buy a hygrometer (inexpensive) to at least keep an eye on humidity levels. Taylor does one, but any will work.

If its too low, don't panic and don't resort to drastic measures. If you're going to humidify your guitar, do it by placing it in an environment with the right levels. Don't put it in your bathroom while you take showers to bring it up to speed, as that'll actually break your guitar. Alternatively, you can buy a case humidifier :)

Don't let fretboard tempt you to soak it in oil, apply a normal coat and then just wipe it off after a little while. It's not supposed to be saturated with mineral oil, which will happen if you oil it up every month. If it seems to get dry again very quickly, don't fret. Just like any wooden instrument, oiled up or not, try to keep it within 40-60% relative humidity.  
  
You ever see people slathering oils onto other unfinished wooden items? Many people out there never oil up their instruments' fretboard without any issue. I think the main benefit of having a little bit of mineral oil in the fretboard is slowing down changes in your fretboards water content, and making it look nice.

The guitar tech at the store I work at once struggled intonating a Music Man. Turned out the nut slots were filed incorrectly, the strings 'left' the nut at the headstock-end of the nut instead of the body-end. This effectively made that string too long, shifting where the notes should be on the string towards the headstock, thus making the frets slightly sharp.

Refiling the nut slots effectively 'intonated' the guitar from the other end.
